locations.name: Brisbane
locations.depot: our own yard at 51–55 Bromley Street, Cornubia, with stock also drawn from the Port of Brisbane at Fisherman Islands and the Wacol–Richlands depot corridor
locations.leadTime: Usually 2–4 business days from order to on the ground, and often next day on the southside
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft where there is a straight run in; crane truck for 40ft, high-set houses and anything that has to go over a fence
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Brisbane, delivered from our Cornubia yard. Come and look at the actual unit before it goes on your block.
locations.line: Brisbane is where our yard is, so the container you buy here is usually one you can walk up to and open before it goes anywhere. That takes the guesswork out of the easy half of the job. The hard half is the ten metres between the kerb and the spot you have picked, because this city was laid out across ridges, gullies and old river bends, and a great many of its best blocks were surveyed when the biggest thing anyone expected down the street was a coal lorry and a milk cart.
locations.uses: lock-up storage on the narrow infill lots going up through Nundah, Cannon Hill and Wooloowin, tool and materials stores for the trades working the constant knockdown-rebuild run across Bulimba, Camp Hill and Ashgrove, parts and stock overflow on the industrial estates at Acacia Ridge, Darra, Eagle Farm and Hemmant, somewhere dry for a whole household while a Queenslander is lifted and built in underneath, workshop and home-gym conversions on blocks where a shed would mean pouring a slab first, and feed, tack and machinery storage out on the acreage fringe through Pullenvale, Cedar Creek and Mount Nebo
access: Work outward from Cornubia and Brisbane sorts itself into a handful of different jobs. The southern arc — Springwood, Rochedale, Daisy Hill, Shailer Park, Loganholme and around to the bay at Victoria Point — is a short hop off the M1 and those drops are the easiest in the city to schedule tightly. North of the river the truck is on the Gateway or the inner-city bypass, which is fine but expensive in time, so an Aspley or Ferny Grove job wants a morning rather than a slot wedged between two others. Inner-city addresses get run early, because a rigid truck with six metres of steel on the back and nowhere legal to stand is not a lunchtime proposition. Then there is the terrain, which is why we ask questions. On the ridges west and north of the river — Bardon, Red Hill, Paddington, Toowong, Chapel Hill, Everton Hills — three things tend to arrive together. The driveway falls away so sharply at the kerb that the truck bed drags before the load is anywhere near clear. The house is up on stumps, so the only ground worth using is out the back or in underneath. And there is fifty-odd years of fig, poinciana and jacaranda leaning out over the carriageway at exactly the height a lifted bed wants to occupy. Any one of those is workable. All three at once is a crane truck, and that is a decision far better made at the quote than at seven in the morning. Ground is the third variable. Through the old river flats at Rocklea, Oxley, Fairfield, Tennyson and along the Breakfast Creek and Kedron Brook corridors the soil is alluvial silt, which sets up like a slab through September and then loses its nerve after a fortnight of storms. New estate fill in the outer north does the same until it has had a summer or two on it. Send us a shot from the middle of the road looking in, one down the length of the approach and one of the ground itself, and we will tell you which truck is coming before anyone talks price.

sections.h: Come and see it at Cornubia before you buy it
p: Our yard is at 51–55 Bromley Street, Cornubia, about half an hour south-east of the CBD straight off the M1. It is a real yard with signage, hardstand and containers standing where you can walk the length of them, swing the doors, put your head inside and look down the floor. That is worth more than any description we could write. Ring first so somebody is there to walk you round and so the unit you are interested in is not buried three deep behind something else, and give yourself twenty minutes rather than five — most people change their mind about size once they are standing next to a 20ft and a 40ft side by side. It is also the quickest way to settle whether a standard height or a high cube is the one you actually want.

Being local also changes what happens when something goes sideways. A Brisbane customer whose driveway has gone soft, or who has picked a size that will not clear the side gate, is a short run from us rather than a full day's cartage from another city. We can pull the booking, swap the unit or come back later in the week without it turning into a saga. Stock moves between Cornubia, the port depots at Fisherman Islands and the yards strung along the Ipswich Motorway through Wacol and Richlands, which is why Brisbane buyers usually get genuine choice of size, height and door configuration rather than whatever single unit happens to be standing free. Ask what has landed recently and we will tell you straight.

sections.h: High-set houses and the crane decision
p: The classic Brisbane back yard is behind a house that sits a metre and a half off the ground on stumps, at the end of a driveway that was poured for a Kingswood. There is often a perfectly good flat spot at the rear. There is just no way to drive to it. That is not a difficult delivery, it is simply a different one: a crane truck stands out the front, picks the container up and places it over the fence, the carport or the roofline, and the whole thing takes less time on site than threading a tilt-tray down a side passage would have. Nine times in ten the container ends up exactly where the owner wanted it, it just arrives over the top rather than through the gate.

What decides whether it works is reach and what is in the air. A crane's capacity drops away sharply the further the boom goes out, so a container travelling eight metres over a paling fence is a very different machine to the same container going twenty-two metres over a two-storey Queenslander. Overhead services across the frontage matter, and so does street width, because the outriggers want solid, even ground and they plant themselves well outside the width of the truck. On the narrow older streets around Highgate Hill, New Farm and Wilston that can mean standing in the road for half an hour with the neighbours warned in advance. Three photos — from the gate at the house, from the back yard looking toward the street, and one straight up at the power lines — settle nearly every one of these questions in a single phone call. Where the answer is genuinely no, it is usually because the only path is over the house and the reach is not there. In that case two 10ft units, or a 20ft where a 40ft was the plan, will very often solve the same storage problem with a much simpler lift.

sections.h: Silt, storms and what goes under the corners
p: A container carries its entire weight, and everything you put in it, through four castings the size of a dinner plate. On Brisbane's old river silt and on young estate fill, that concentration is what causes trouble. The unit goes down in dry weather onto ground that feels like concrete, a summer storm cell parks over the suburb for an hour, and one corner quietly gives up a hundred millimetres while the other three stay put. A container that is out of square is a container whose doors have to be shouldered, and the doors are the only part of it you actually touch, so a good store turns into a daily irritation and then into a bill. None of that is the container's fault and none of it is hard to avoid.

Four hardwood sleepers or concrete pads under the castings, bedded level and checked on both diagonals, prevents all of it and costs almost nothing. Set the doors at the top of any fall so they open with the slope working for you rather than dragging on the latch. Keep the underside clear so air moves and water gets away rather than sitting against the floor bearers, And if it is landing under a fig or a gum, get up there twice a year and clear the roof, because a mat of wet leaves sitting on a panel does more damage over ten years than the weather ever will. Tell us at the quote what the ground is — slab, turf over clay, sand, fresh fill, or unknown — and the packing rides out on the truck with the container so the levelling gets done while we are there, not left behind for you.

faqs.q: Can I look at the container before I buy it in Brisbane?
faqs.a: Yes, and we would rather you did. The yard is at 51–55 Bromley Street, Cornubia, roughly thirty minutes south-east of the CBD off the M1, with the units standing on hardstand so you can swing the doors, walk the floor and run your eye over the seals yourself. Ring ahead so somebody is there and the unit you want to see is accessible rather than stacked behind something. If the trip does not suit, ask for photos of the actual unit on request and they come through before delivery: corners, door end, roof, and the floor shot from the inside.

faqs.q: My driveway at Paddington is steep and the house is high-set. Can you still deliver?
faqs.a: Usually, but not on a tilt-tray. Where the drive pitches down hard at the kerb the truck bed grounds before the container is clear, and a high-set house means the only usable ground is out the back where a truck cannot reach anyway. Those blocks are craned: the truck stands on the street and places the container over the fence or the carport. What we need to know is how far it has to travel horizontally, what height it has to clear, and whether there are service lines across your frontage. A photo from the middle of the road and one from the back yard will normally answer it in a single call.

faqs.q: How quickly can you get a container onto a Brisbane block?
faqs.a: Two to four business days is the normal window, and southside addresses within reach of Cornubia are frequently next business day on a standard 20ft with clear access. What adds time is a crane booking, a unit that has to come across from a port depot first, or wet weather on silt or fresh fill where waiting two days beats leaving a pair of ruts across your lawn. If you are working to a fixed date — a settlement, a removalist, a site start — say so at the enquiry and we will build the run around it instead of telling you afterwards that it did not fit.

faqs.q: Do I need approval to put a container on a residential block in Brisbane?
faqs.a: That turns on a few things: the length of stay, whether the unit is visible from the road, what goes inside it, and whether the property sits under a character or heritage overlay, which plenty of the inner suburbs do. Newer estates frequently layer a covenant on top that is tighter than anything the council asks for. We are not going to guess your street's position — that one is worth confirming yourself before you order. The pattern is consistent enough to plan around, though: temporary, screened and used for storage is the easy end, permanent and prominent from the road is where the questions start.

locations.name: Sydney
locations.depot: container depots behind Port Botany, with stock also drawn from the yards through Chullora, Yennora and the Erskine Park corridor
locations.leadTime: Usually 3–5 business days from order to on the ground
locations.truck: Tilt-tray where there is a straight run in off the street; crane truck for terraces, strata sites and anything without side access
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire across Sydney, supplied off Port Botany. Terraces, strata sites and crane lifts scoped before we book a truck.
locations.line: Sydney has no shortage of containers. Port Botany moves more boxes than anywhere in the country and the depots behind it hold real depth in every common size, so choice is rarely what holds a job up. The city is what holds it up. Sydney was built on sandstone around a harbour, and the result is narrow streets, split-level blocks, strata buildings, benched driveways and back yards you cannot see from the road. Almost every hard job here reduces to two questions: where can the truck legally stand, and how does the container get from there to the spot.
locations.uses: site stores on the relentless knockdown-rebuild run through the Shire, Ryde and the Hills, tool and materials lock-ups for the trades working out of Smithfield, Wetherill Park, Ingleburn and Seven Hills, strata storage where a basement ran out of room a decade ago, film, event and festival gear that lives in a box between shoots, boat, board and dive gear on the northern beaches where the garage lost that argument long ago, stock overflow for small businesses squeezed by inner-west warehouse rents, and feed, fencing and machinery storage on the acreage through Kenthurst, Dural, Bringelly and the Hawkesbury flats
access: The single most useful thing you can tell us about a Sydney delivery is what the frontage looks like, because the container is almost never the constraint. In the inner west and inner east — Newtown, Erskineville, Annandale, Balmain, Paddington, Surry Hills — the housing is terraces with no side access whatsoever, a rear lane if you are lucky, and streets where a truck standing still blocks the whole carriageway. Many of those streets are clearways or peak-hour restricted, which pins the delivery to a mid-morning or mid-afternoon window rather than whenever suits. Standing a crane on a public road generally means notice to the council and sometimes a permit, and that timeframe is theirs rather than ours, so start early. On the north shore and the northern beaches the problem changes shape. Avalon, Newport, Bilgola, Killara and the streets running off the ridgelines are benched into sandstone, which gives you a driveway with a severe crest at the kerb, a hard turn halfway down, and a garage under the house. Sandstone is superb bearing ground and awful to manoeuvre on. Add mature canopy that councils across the north are protective of, and the honest answer on some of those blocks is a smaller unit than you first wanted. Out west the ground changes again. Through Blacktown, Kellyville, Penrith and Camden you are on shale-derived reactive clay that swells through a wet winter and shrinks back hard in February, and it does not move evenly across a block. Down near the port and out to Kurnell and Cronulla it is sand, which drains beautifully and carries very little. The newer estates at Marsden Park, Oran Park, Box Hill and Leppington bring the familiar pattern of narrow carriageways, cars parked both sides, stormwater grates and comms pits on the kerb line that a loaded rear axle will crack, and cut-and-fill blocks that have not finished settling. On the Hawkesbury flats around Windsor, Pitt Town and Richmond the alluvial soil is excellent and the water is the thing to plan for. Photos from the street, along the approach and of the spot answer nearly all of it.

sections.h: Terraces, strata and lifting over the roof
p: A very large share of Sydney housing has no side access at all, and that is normal rather than a problem. The container goes over the top. A crane truck sets up on the street, lifts the unit over the terrace or the townhouse and places it in the courtyard or the back yard. The three things that decide feasibility are reach, clearance and the road. Reach, because a crane's lifting capacity falls away steeply as the boom extends, so twenty-two metres over a two-storey house is a much larger machine than eight metres over a rear fence. Clearance, because power and comms lines across the frontage, a pergola, a mature plane tree or a pool cage all have to be gone over rather than through. And the road, because outriggers need a footprint wider than the truck on firm level ground, which on a one-way inner-west street means occupying the whole carriageway for a period.

Strata and unit blocks add an administrative layer that is easy to underestimate. Buildings typically want written approval, a nominated delivery window, proof of insurance from whoever is carting it, and a route that avoids a basement with a clearance no truck is ever going to meet. None of that is hard. All of it is close to impossible to arrange on the morning of delivery. Get the approval and the window in hand first, then let us book the truck to land inside it. If your building has a loading dock and a booking system, tell us at the quote and we will work to it. Townhouse complexes and ground-floor apartments with a shared driveway want the same treatment, because the truck has to stand somewhere that does not block every other resident for the morning.

Sydney gives you three quite different grounds inside an hour's drive, and each one wants the same fix for a different reason. Sandstone through the harbour suburbs and along the northern ridgelines is as good a bearing surface as you will find, but it is almost never level and it will not let you dig a pad in without effort, so the answer is to build the low side up rather than cut the high side out. Digging the high side out only leaves a trench for water to run down and sit in against the steel. Reactive shale clay across the west and south-west takes up water through winter and shrinks back through summer, unevenly, and a container placed straight onto it will follow that movement one corner at a time and never come back. Coastal and Botany-side sand drains fast and carries badly, so a corner casting concentrating a couple of tonne will simply push down into it.

In all three cases the remedy is four hardwood sleepers or concrete pads under the corner castings, bedded level and checked on both diagonals, with the door end sitting on the high side of any fall. Get the floor a hundred millimetres or so clear of the ground so air moves underneath and the underside is not sitting against damp soil for a decade. It also makes the container far easier to lift out again later, which matters more than people expect on a Sydney block that will probably be redeveloped inside twenty years. Whichever of the three grounds you are on, mention it at the quote and we will bring the packing on the truck rather than leaving you a job for the weekend.

sections.h: Booking around a Sydney working day
p: Distance is not what makes a Sydney delivery slow. Windows are. A truck coming out of a Port Botany depot to Castle Hill, Penrith or Helensburgh is committed to a run that has to clear the clearways at each end, dodge the tunnels and the toll network sensibly, and still have time to set up and unload in daylight. That is why we schedule the metro work in blocks and why a firm morning slot on a tight street is worth asking for rather than assuming. Three to five business days from order to on the ground is what to plan for, and a crane booking, a strata window or a council permit will push the far end of it out.

The most useful thing you can do is give us the constraints at the enquiry rather than at the door. Whether the street is a clearway and when. Whether the building has a nominated delivery time. Whether the neighbours can be asked to move two cars off the frontage for an hour, which on a narrow inner-west street is frequently the entire difference between the job going in and the truck going home. Whether there is a gate, and what it measures at the narrowest point rather than at the posts. Tell us those four things and a Sydney delivery becomes ordinary. The more of it we know before the truck is loaded, the less of it turns into a problem on the day.

faqs.q: There is no side access to my terrace. Can you still get a container into the back yard?
faqs.a: Usually yes, by lifting it over. A crane truck stands on the street and places the container in the courtyard or the yard, which is routine across the inner west and inner east where side access simply does not exist. What decides it is how far the container has to travel horizontally, what it has to clear on the way, whether power or comms lines cross the frontage, and whether the street leaves room to plant the outriggers. Shots from the front gate, from the back yard looking toward the street, and one straight up at the lines will usually get you a straight answer on the phone.

faqs.q: Do I need council or strata approval for a container in Sydney?
faqs.a: For a unit block or a strata property, almost certainly, and it is worth starting early, because getting the approval and getting a delivery slot are two different queues. For a house, it comes down to length of stay, visibility from the road and what the container is used for, and the answer differs council to council. If a crane has to stand on a public road, councils generally want notice and may require a permit, and that timeframe is theirs. We will not guess at the rule for your address — check it before you order, then tell us the window you have been given and we will work inside it.

faqs.q: Can I inspect a container at the Port Botany depot before delivery?
faqs.a: Not generally, and it is fairer to say so plainly. The depots that hold Sydney stock are third-party facilities running heavy machinery all day and they are not set up for the public to walk through. What we do instead is send photos of the specific unit on request before delivery — corners, door end, roof and the internal floor — so you know exactly what is coming rather than a stock image of something similar. If you want more, ask for a particular angle and we will get it.

faqs.q: How far out of Sydney will you deliver?
faqs.a: Right across the basin and well beyond it — the Hawkesbury, the Blue Mountains, the Southern Highlands, the Illawarra and up the Central Coast are all normal work. What changes with distance is scheduling rather than capability, because runs past the metro get planned around the route rather than slotted into a day. The mountains and the Illawarra escarpment also bring steep, narrow approaches where the size question is worth settling first. Send the address and a photo taken from the road looking at your entrance and we will tell you what can physically get there.

locations.name: Melbourne
locations.depot: the Port of Melbourne and the container depot belt through Altona, Laverton and Truganina, with stock also held out through Dandenong South
locations.leadTime: Usually 3–5 business days; wet-winter drops onto soft ground get scheduled with a little slack
locations.truck: Tilt-tray where the street and the run in allow it; crane truck for terraces, laneway sites and anything under a canopy or near overhead wiring
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Melbourne, off the port and the Altona depots. Laneways, tram wires and reactive clay planned for properly.
locations.line: Melbourne is an easy city to supply and a genuinely awkward one to deliver into, and the awkwardness is at least predictable. Boxes come off the wharves and sit in the depot belt through Altona, Laverton and Truganina, so getting hold of the right size is straightforward. Getting it behind a single-fronted terrace in Fitzroy with a bluestone lane and overhead wiring, or onto a Tarneit block sitting on clay that swells all winter and shrinks all summer, is where the actual work is. That is the part worth talking through before you order.
locations.uses: gear and stock storage for trades working out of Dandenong South, Campbellfield, Braeside and Truganina, site stores on the knockdown-rebuild run through Bentleigh, Balwyn, Essendon and Ivanhoe, somewhere to put an entire period home while it is restumped and reworked over six months, workshop and studio conversions on hills blocks at Olinda, Kallista and Belgrave, vineyard, orchard and equipment storage through the Yarra Valley and around Coldstream, market and event stock that only surfaces at weekends, and hay, tack and machinery storage on the small holdings around Macedon, Whittlesea and Bacchus Marsh
access: Three things shape a Melbourne delivery more than anything else. The first is the inner-suburban street pattern. Fitzroy, Collingwood, Richmond, Carlton, Brunswick, Port Melbourne and South Melbourne are single-fronted terraces with no side access and a bluestone rear lane behind them. Those lanes are narrow, often one-way, frequently obstructed by wheelie bins and parked cars, and the surface is dished to a centre drain that a long rigid truck will bottom out on. Sometimes the lane is the answer and sometimes the answer is a lift from the street over the roofline. The second is overhead wiring, and it is the constraint people forget. Melbourne's tram network carries live overhead traction wire down the middle of a great many inner arterials — Sydney Road, Nicholson Street, Glenferrie Road, Chapel Street, High Street — and no crane goes anywhere near it. On a tram street the lift has to happen well clear of the wires or the job moves to a side street and a longer reach, and that gets worked out on a map before a truck is booked, not on arrival. The third is ground, and Melbourne has two very different sorts. West and north across the basalt plain — Werribee, Point Cook, Tarneit, Truganina, Craigieburn, Sunbury — the soil is highly reactive clay. It takes up water through a long wet winter and swells, then gives it back through summer and shrinks away, and the seasonal movement is significant enough that houses out there are engineered for it. A container placed straight onto that ground will follow it, one corner at a time. Down through the south-eastern sand belt — Moorabbin, Cheltenham, Braeside, Mordialloc, Frankston — you get the opposite: free-draining sand that carries very little and will let a corner casting straight through thin turf. Then there are the ranges. Olinda, Sassafras, Kallista, Belgrave, Monbulk and the Kinglake side are narrow, steeply cambered and hairpinned, running under mature mountain ash with low limbs and long stretches with a bank on one side and nothing on the other. A 20ft on a tilt-tray manages those climbs. A 40ft is a conversation before it is a booking.

sections.h: Laneways, terraces and live overhead wire
p: The inner suburbs are the most common source of Melbourne enquiries and the least suited to a truck. A single-fronted terrace in Fitzroy or Richmond has a two-metre frontage, no side passage and a back yard the size of a car space, reached by a bluestone lane that was built for a nightcart. Where the lane is genuinely usable, a small tilt-tray or a hiab can often work down it, though the dished centre and the camber against the fences limit what will physically fit. Where it is not, the container goes over the top from the street with a crane truck, and the questions are the same as anywhere: reach, height to clear, what is overhead and whether the road gives room for the outriggers.

Overhead traction wiring is the one Melbourne-specific answer we will not bend on. If the property fronts a tram route, the lift does not happen under the wires. Sometimes that means setting up on the cross street and reaching further, sometimes it means using the rear lane after all, and occasionally it means a smaller container is the only workable option. It is far better to establish that at the quote than to have a crane truck sitting on Sydney Road with nowhere legal to boom. Send a photo from the middle of the road looking at the house, one along the rear lane if there is one, and one looking up, and we can usually settle it in one phone call.

sections.h: Reactive clay on the basalt plain
p: If your address is in the western or northern growth corridor, the ground is the thing to get right and everything else is detail. The clay out through Wyndham, Melton and the Hume corridor is among the more reactive soil in the country. It swells with winter rain and shrinks back through a dry February, it does not do either evenly across a block, and a new estate lot has usually been cut and filled on top of that and has not finished consolidating. Drop a container straight onto turf out there and it will rack. A racked container is one whose doors need a shoulder and then a crowbar, and since the doors are the only part of it you ever interact with, that is the difference between a good store and a standing annoyance.

The fix is unglamorous and permanent. Four concrete pads or hardwood sleepers set into the ground under the castings, bedded down and checked corner to corner so all four sit at one height. Door end on the high side of any fall. Underside kept clear so air moves and water gets away instead of pooling against the floor bearers. Tell us the ground type at the quote — slab, turf over clay, fresh fill, sand — and the timber comes on the truck and the levelling happens as part of the delivery. If your block has a designed overland flow path across it, which most estate lots do, mention that as well, because a six-metre steel box parked in the middle of it will send water somewhere the builder did not intend.

sections.h: Winter, and why July is not October
p: Melbourne differs from the northern capitals in a way that genuinely changes delivery planning. Up north a wet block dries out in two days of sun. Here, a paddock or an unsealed driveway that goes soft in late May can stay soft until September, because the rain arrives in modest amounts over a long time and the evaporation is not there to take it away. That matters on acreage through the Macedon Ranges, Yarra Valley, Whittlesea and Bacchus Marsh, on any long gravel driveway, and on new estate blocks where the turf is thin and the fill is young. The same goes for a shaded south-facing yard in the inner suburbs, which can hold water for weeks after the rain has stopped.

So we plan winter rural work with a bit of slack in it and we will ring and move a booking rather than commit a loaded truck to a driveway it cannot back out of. Nobody wins from a bogged truck — not you, watching it cut a trench across the paddock, and not us, with a driver and a machine tied up for the day. Where a block is marginal, the usual answer is to leave the container on solid ground near the road for you to drag in with a tractor when it suits, or to send a crane truck that can sit on the sealed part of the drive and reach further in than a tilt-tray ever could. If you have a spot that stays solid no matter the season, tell us where it is at the booking. Local knowledge from the person who lives there beats anything we can read off a map.

faqs.q: Can you deliver a container down a bluestone rear lane in Fitzroy or Richmond?
faqs.a: Sometimes, and it depends on the lane rather than the container. The inner-suburban lanes are narrow, often one-way, usually part-blocked by bins and parked cars, and dished to a centre drain that a long rigid truck will ground on. Where a lane is genuinely usable we will use it, generally with a smaller unit. Where it is not, the container is lifted from the street over the house instead. Send a photo down the lane from both ends and one from the street looking at the property and we will tell you which of the two it is.

faqs.q: Will tram wires stop a crane delivery in inner Melbourne?
faqs.a: They will stop it happening directly under them, yes. Overhead traction wire is live and no crane works near it, so if your property fronts a tram route the lift has to be set up clear of the wires — often from a cross street with a longer reach, sometimes from a rear lane instead. Occasionally it means a smaller container is the only option that works. This is the sort of thing that has to be planned at the quote rather than discovered by a driver on Sydney Road, so tell us the street and we will look at it before anything is booked.

faqs.q: Can you get a 40ft container up to Olinda, Sassafras or Belgrave?
faqs.a: Sometimes, but the roads decide it, not us. The climbs into the Dandenongs are narrow and steeply cambered with tight hairpins, mature mountain ash hanging low over the carriageway and long sections with a bank on one side and a drop on the other. A 20ft on a tilt-tray goes up there routinely. A 40ft means checking the approach and the gate first, and on a few of those roads the real answer is a pair of 20ft units end to end, which normally buys you more usable space and a far simpler delivery anyway.

faqs.q: Can I see the container before it is delivered in Melbourne?
faqs.a: Not in person — the depots holding Melbourne stock are third-party facilities running heavy machinery, and they are not set up for the public to wander through. What we do instead is send photos of the actual unit on request before delivery, covering the corners, the door end, the roof and the internal floor, so you are looking at the container you are getting rather than a photo of one like it. If a cargo-worthy unit is what you need, it is checked wind and watertight before it leaves the yard; the grades page sets out what each grade is checked for.

locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft on most Perth blocks; crane truck for 40ft, hills sites and anything going over a fence
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Perth, held at our Fremantle depot. Sand, limestone and the scarp allowed for before we book a truck.
locations.line: Perth runs on its own supply and it pays to understand what that means. The stock we sell here sits at a depot in Fremantle, because carting a container across the Nullarbor costs more than any sensible person would want to pay for a steel box. Two things follow. What is standing in Fremantle this week is what you can actually have this week, so ringing early is worth more in Perth than in any other city we serve. And once it is yours, the run out to almost any metropolitan address is short, flat and quick.
locations.uses: lock-up storage on the big new lots at Alkimos, Yanchep, Baldivis and Byford, tool and plant stores for the trades and mining services businesses at Kwinana, Naval Base, Bibra Lake, Malaga and Henderson, somewhere for a shed's worth of gear while people work away on a swing roster, boat, dive and camping storage where the garage was full three years ago, dry storage for market gardeners and small growers on the Wanneroo and Gnangara sands, feed, tack and machinery storage on the hills blocks through Roleystone, Chidlow and Gidgegannup, and vineyard and equipment storage out through the Swan Valley
access: Perth is one of the more forgiving capitals to drive a truck around and one of the less forgiving to stand a container on. The metropolitan roads are wide, the grid is generous, the estates are newer and there is very little of the constricted inner-city street pattern that makes the eastern capitals difficult. Then you get to the block. Almost all of Perth sits on the Swan Coastal Plain, which is sand — Bassendean sand through the inland suburbs, and Spearwood sand over Tamala limestone as you move toward the coast. Dry sand carries almost nothing. A loaded truck will sit its rear duals into a nature strip that looked entirely solid, and a corner casting concentrating a couple of tonne will disappear into thin turf inside a season. Nearer the coast, from Scarborough and Trigg down through Cottesloe, Fremantle and Coogee, limestone often sits close to the surface, which is excellent bearing but rarely level and stubborn to dig a pad into. Wind is the other thing that is genuinely local. Through the warmer months the sea breeze comes in off the Indian Ocean from around the middle of the day and it comes in with real force. A container hanging off a crane is a large flat sail, so afternoon lifts on exposed coastal blocks are the ones that get moved to the morning, and we would rather schedule around that than argue with it on site. Inland and up on the scarp the day runs the other way, with dry heat, dust and firm ground for most of the year. The Darling Scarp is the third factor. Kalamunda, Gooseberry Hill, Roleystone, Bickley, Mundaring and the Chidlow side are steep, winding and narrow, with granite outcrops, tall jarrah and marri canopy over the road and driveways cut hard into the fall. A 20ft goes up there comfortably. A 40ft needs the approach and the turning space checked before anyone commits a truck to a climb it may have to reverse back down.

sections.h: Why Perth stock is Perth stock
p: It is worth being straight about how supply works on this side of the country, because it changes how you should approach buying. There is no realistic way to shuttle a container over from the east for an individual customer — the cartage across the Nullarbor is a large multiple of what the box is worth, and anyone who tells you otherwise is quietly building it into a number somewhere. So what we sell in Perth is what is on the ground at our Fremantle depot. In practice the range is good and covers the common sizes and grades. What it does not do is respond instantly to an unusual request, so if you want something specific — a particular height, a door configuration, a set number of matching units for a project — start the conversation two or three weeks out rather than two or three days.

The upside of a single local holding point is that everything after the phone call is short. Fremantle to Joondalup, Armadale, Midland or Rockingham is an easy run on good roads, and the whole metropolitan area is reachable inside a morning. Inspection at Fremantle is by arrangement rather than a walk-in, because it is a working depot with machines moving all day. Ring, tell us what you are after, and we will set a time when someone can walk you to the unit and open it up for you. If a trip across town is not practical, ask and we will send photos of the actual container on request before delivery. Give us a couple of days' notice for an inspection and it is straightforward to organise.

sections.h: Sand, limestone and four corners at the same height
p: Perth ground is the reason a container goes wrong here, and it is entirely preventable. On sand the problem is bearing. The unit puts everything it weighs through four castings, and sand simply moves out of the way underneath them — unevenly, because one corner will always find a looser pocket than the others. Within a season the frame is out of square and the doors have started to bind. Concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under the four corners, bedded down into firm sand rather than sitting on the surface, spread that load and settle the question for good. On limestone country the issue is the opposite. The bearing is superb and the ground will not oblige you by being flat, so the right approach is to pack the low side up to meet the high side rather than trying to chip the high side down, which only ever produces a channel for water to sit in.

Either way, get the floor a hundred millimetres or so off the ground so air moves underneath, hang the door end off the high side of any fall so the doors are not fighting the slope, and keep the grass down around the bottom rail. On the coastal strip that last one matters more than most people expect: it is long wet grass and leaf litter holding moisture against the steel that starts surface corrosion, far more than salt air on its own. Tell us what the ground is at the quote and we will bring the packing on the truck and level it as part of the delivery. Done properly on the day it lands, that setup never needs revisiting for the life of the container.

sections.h: Up the scarp, out to the country
p: The hills are the one part of metropolitan Perth where the size question needs settling before anything else. The climbs to Kalamunda, Gooseberry Hill, Roleystone and Mundaring are narrow and winding with granite either side, low jarrah and marri limbs across the carriageway and driveways that fall away hard off a road with no shoulder to speak of. A truck that cannot make a bend up there has to reverse a long way downhill, and a container that will not fit through a gate at the top has to go all the way back to Fremantle. Five minutes with an aerial view of the drive and the gate, and one photo taken from the gate looking back down the road, heads off nearly all of that. A 20ft is the sensible workhorse for hills blocks; where the length really is needed, a pair of 20ft units butted together beats forcing a 40ft up a road that does not want one.

Beyond the metropolitan area the same logic applies with distance added. The Peel region, the Avon Valley, the Wheatbelt and the south-west are all serviced, but those runs are scheduled around the route rather than dropped into a day, so a hard date needs saying at the enquiry rather than confirming later. Farm and rural-residential deliveries bring the usual list of things worth mentioning up front: the gate width measured at its narrowest point rather than at the posts, any grid and whether anyone knows what it is rated to, the state of the driveway surface, powerlines to a pump shed or a house, and whether there is genuine truck-sized turning room at the far end. Tell us those at the booking and it is a non-event.

faqs.q: Can I inspect a container in Perth before buying it?
faqs.a: Yes, by arrangement. Our Perth stock is held at a depot in Fremantle, and because it is a working yard with machinery moving all day it is not somewhere you can simply turn up and wander through. Ring us, tell us the size and grade you are looking at, and we will book a time when someone can take you to the unit, open the doors and let you look down the floor and check the seals properly. If getting across town is not practical, we will send photos of the actual container on request before delivery — corners, door end, roof and internal floor.

faqs.q: How long does delivery take in Perth?
faqs.a: Three to seven business days is the usual window, and where it lands in that range depends mostly on what is standing at Fremantle when you order. Once the unit is allocated, the run to a metropolitan address is short. What stretches it out is a crane booking, a request for something less common in size or configuration, or a delivery beyond the metro that has to be scheduled around a route. If you are working to a fixed date, say so at the enquiry — with Perth supply being local and finite, early notice is genuinely the thing that gets you what you want.

faqs.q: Will a container sink into sand on a Perth block?
faqs.a: Placed straight onto sand or thin turf it will go down unevenly, because every casting drives its share of the load into a patch the size of a dinner plate and sand does very little to resist it. Concrete pads or hardwood sleepers under the four corners, bedded into firm sand rather than laid on the surface and checked level on both diagonals, fix it permanently for very little money. Closer to the coast where limestone sits near the surface, the bearing is excellent but the ground is uneven, so the right approach is to pack the low side up rather than cut the high side away.

faqs.q: Can you deliver up to Kalamunda, Roleystone or out to the Swan Valley?
faqs.a: Regularly. The Swan Valley is flat, open and about as easy as delivery gets. The scarp is a different proposition — narrow winding climbs, granite, low jarrah canopy over the road and steep driveways cut into the fall — so the size question is worth settling before you order. A 20ft goes up comfortably. A 40ft needs the approach, the gate and the turning space checked first, and on some of those roads two 20ft is the better answer. Send us the address and a photo from your gate looking back toward the road and we will give you a straight answer.
